title: Drone-Delivered Gel Speeds Healing on Ukraine's Front Lines
summary:
A wound and burn treatment developed in Calgary, Canada, is now being delivered by drone to help wounded soldiers and civilians in Ukraine. The treatment, called NanoSALV Catalytic, was made by the Calgary company NanoTess and first received Health Canada approval in 2022. It was first evaluated by treating unhoused people living in encampments, and it is now being used for military purposes.

"We actually started this company with a grant from National Defence back in 2020 and then have had it come full circle here in 2026 to now be used in the front lines within Ukraine," said NanoTess co-founder and CEO Megan Leslie.

The catalyst sits in a lightweight, non-flammable gel applied directly to a wound. It can be flown by drone to the front line and used by people with limited medical training. In use on the Ukrainian front lines since June, it has treated 6,000 wounded soldiers and civilians. Its nanomaterials speed up the body's natural healing, lower the energy healing requires, and fight germs and other infection-causing micro-organisms.

Clinical pharmacist Hailie Uren, an Australian who has spent four years in eastern Ukraine working for the Ukrainian Ministry of Health, said the treatment is critical for buying time: it can be applied and go to work when a single nurse must care for up to 90 patients. "That wound can heal without consistent nursing intervention," she said. Uren said the gel is so in demand that other patients try to find wounds just so she can use it on them too.

The gel has also been used back home in Canada, after a wildfire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright killed four soldiers and burned dozens more.
why_it_matters: When medical help is scarce, a treatment that works quickly and with little training can save lives and ease pressure on nurses. It also shows how a civilian medical invention can be adapted for war zones and disaster scenes.

background_read: When skin is cut or burned, the body must close the wound and fight off germs, which takes time and energy.
In a war zone or after a wildfire, many injured people may need care at once, while trained medical workers and supplies can be hard to reach.
A light gel that can be flown by drone and put straight on a wound could help injured people sooner, even where nurses are stretched thin.
That is why a treatment that speeds healing and keeps working without constant nursing care matters on a front line.
